hints: Start from atomic number 29 and recall why copper does not follow the simple $4s^2 3d^9$ filling order, think about the stability of a full $3d$ subshell.
Remember that when a transition metal forms a positive ion, electrons are removed from the $4s$ orbital before the $3d$ orbital.
walkthrough:
Build the copper atom**
Copper has 29 electrons. Filling up to argon accounts for 18, leaving 11 to place. You might expect $[Ar] 3d^9 4s^2$, but moving one $4s$ electron into $3d$ gives a completely full $3d^{10}$ subshell plus a half filled $4s^1$, which is lower in energy. So you get $[Ar] 3d^{10}4s^1$.

Form the $Cu^{2+}$ ion**
When making cations, always remove $4s$ electrons first, then $3d$. Copper loses its single $4s$ electron first, then one $3d$ electron to make the 2+ charge. That leaves $[Ar] 3d^9$ with an empty $4s$.

Final answer: copper atom: [Ar] $3d^{10}4s^1$
$\text{Cu}^{2+}$: [Ar] $3d^9$

hints: Look at what is happening to the ligands around copper, water molecules are being swapped for chloride ions with no change in oxidation state.
walkthrough:
Spot the swap**
On the left copper is surrounded by six $\text{H}_2\text{O}$ ligands. On the right it is surrounded by four $\text{Cl}^-$ ligands. The copper stays as +2 throughout, no redox and no change in coordination chemistry other than the identity of the ligands. That is the classic signature of ligand exchange, also called ligand substitution.
Final answer: ligand exchange (ligand substitution / replacement / displacement)

hints: Recall the very familiar blue solution of hydrated copper(II) and the colour change seen when concentrated hydrochloric acid is added.
walkthrough:
Link formula to familiar colour**
$[\text{Cu}(\text{H}_2\text{O})_6]^{2+}$ is the standard blue copper(II) solution you see in the lab. Replacing water with chloride to give $[\text{CuCl}_4]^{2-}$ shifts the d-d splitting and the colour changes to yellow or yellow-green, often seen as green in mixtures.
Final answer: $[\text{Cu}(\text{H}_2\text{O})_6]^{2+}$ blue and $[\text{CuCl}_4]^{2-}$ yellow / green (yellow-green)

hints: Count the ligands in $[\text{CuCl}_4]^{2-}$ and recall the two common shapes for coordination number 4, then think which one chloride normally gives with copper(II).
walkthrough:
Use coordination number**
$[\text{CuCl}_4]^{2-}$ has four $\text{Cl}^-$ ligands directly bonded to copper, so coordination number is 4. With four large chloride ligands, repulsion is minimised in a tetrahedral arrangement around the central $\text{Cu}^{2+}$.

hints: Write a $K_c$ style expression with products over reactants, raising each concentration to its stoichiometric coefficient, and remember water is omitted as a pure liquid.
walkthrough:
Construct $K_{stab}$ like $K_c$**
Put the concentration of the product complex $[\text{CuCl}_4^{2-}]$ on top. Put the reactant complex $[\text{Cu}(\text{H}_2\text{O})_6^{2+}]$ times $[\text{Cl}^-]$ raised to the power 4 on the bottom, because four chlorides appear in the balanced equation. $$K_{\text{stab}} = \dfrac{[\text{CuCl}_4^{2-}]}{[\text{Cu}(\text{H}_2\text{O})_6^{2+}][\text{Cl}^-]^4}$$ Water is left out because its concentration is effectively constant.

hints: Break the word bidentate into bi meaning two and dentate meaning teeth or points of attachment to the metal.
Recall how any ligand bonds to a metal, through donation of a lone pair into a vacant metal orbital.
walkthrough:
Picture two points of attachment**
Think of the ligand biting the metal with two teeth. Ethane-1,2-diamine, $\text{H}_2\text{NCH}_2\text{CH}_2\text{NH}_2$, has two nitrogen atoms, each with a lone pair.

Form two dative bonds**
Each nitrogen donates its lone pair into a vacant orbital on $\text{Cu}^{2+}$, forming two coordinate bonds from the same ligand molecule. That is what makes it bidentate.
Final answer: A species that has two lone pairs that each form a coordinate (dative covalent) bond to a central metal ion.

hints: Compare $7.94 \times 10^7$ with $3.98 \times 10^{10}$ and remember larger $K_{stab}$ means more stable product and equilibrium further to the right.
walkthrough:
Compare the numbers**
$K_{stab}$ for $[\text{Cu}(en)(\text{H}_2\text{O})_4]^{2+}$ is $3.98 \times 10^{10}$, about 500 times larger than $7.94 \times 10^7$ for $[\text{Cu}(\text{NH}_3)_2(\text{H}_2\text{O})_4]^{2+}$. A bigger stability constant means the forward reaction is more favoured, so equilibrium 2 lies more to the right. This is the chelate effect of the bidentate ligand.
Final answer: Equilibrium 2 lies further to the right than equilibrium 1 (larger $K_{\text{stab}}$ means more stable complex).

hints: Think about $[\text{Ni}(en)_3]^{2+}$ with three identical bidentate rings arranged octahedrally, it can exist as non-superimposable mirror images like a propeller.
walkthrough:
Recognise chiral propeller**
With three $en$ rings around octahedral nickel, the complex has no plane of symmetry. It exists as two non-superimposable mirror images, just like left and right handed propellers. That is optical isomerism.

hints: Start by sketching an octahedral centre with solid wedges, hashed wedges and straight lines to show 3D geometry around Ni.
Represent each $en$ as an arc linking two adjacent (cis) positions, remember $en$ cannot span trans positions.
Draw the mirror image of your first structure, the two arcs should twist in opposite senses to show the pair of enantiomers.
walkthrough:
Set up octahedral 3D**
Draw Ni in the centre with six $\text{N}$ atoms octahedrally arranged. Use a solid wedge for a bond coming out, a hashed wedge for a bond going back, and normal lines for bonds in the plane. This 3D framework is essential.

Add three $en$ bridges**
Join adjacent N atoms in pairs with a $-\text{CH}_2\text{CH}_2-$ arc to represent each $en$. Each $en$ must occupy two cis positions, forming a five membered chelate ring. Check all six N atoms are used.

Draw the mirror image**
Now draw the exact mirror image, with the chelate arcs twisting the opposite way. The two structures should look like left and right handed propellers and must not be superimposable. Keep wedges and dashes consistent to show true 3D optical isomers.

Final answer: Two 3D octahedral structures of $[\text{Ni}(en)_3]^{2+}$, each showing three $en$ ligands bridging cis positions, drawn as non-superimposable mirror images with correct wedge / dash bonds.

hints: Recall the Bronsted-Lowry definition of a base in terms of protons, not hydroxide ions.
Look at the nitrogen atoms in $\text{H}_2\text{NCH}_2\text{CH}_2\text{NH}_2$ and identify what feature allows them to bond to $\text{H}^+$.
walkthrough:
Recall Bronsted-Lowry**
A Bronsted-Lowry base is a proton acceptor. It takes $\text{H}^+$ from an acid to form its conjugate acid.

Find the acceptor site**
Each $-\text{NH}_2$ group has a nitrogen with a lone pair. That lone pair can form a dative bond to $\text{H}^+$, giving $-\text{NH}_3^+$. Because ethane-1,2-diamine has two such groups, it can accept two protons.
Final answer: The nitrogen atoms have lone pairs that can accept (receive) a proton / $\text{H}^+$.

hints: Since the diamine has two basic $-\text{NH}_2$ groups and HCl is in excess, think how many moles of HCl will react per mole of diamine.
walkthrough:
Protonate both ends**
Excess acid means both amine groups are protonated. Each $-\text{NH}_2$ gains $\text{H}^+$ from $\text{HCl}$ to become $-\text{NH}_3^+$, balanced by $\text{Cl}^-$. $$\text{H}_2\text{NCH}_2\text{CH}_2\text{NH}_2 + 2\text{HCl} \rightarrow \text{ClH}_3\text{NCH}_2\text{CH}_2\text{NH}_3\text{Cl}$$

Final answer: $\text{H}_2\text{NCH}_2\text{CH}_2\text{NH}_2 + 2\text{HCl} \rightarrow [\text{H}_3\text{NCH}_2\text{CH}_2\text{NH}_3]\text{Cl}_2$ (allow $\text{ClH}_3\text{NCH}_2\text{CH}_2\text{NH}_3\text{Cl}$ or ionic form with $2\text{H}^+$)

hints: Identify the functional groups reacting, $-\text{COOH}$ with $-\text{NH}_2$ to make an amide link $-\text{CONH}-$ plus water.
Remember to show two full repeat units linked together with continuation bonds at each end to indicate a polymer chain.
walkthrough:
Make the amide link**
Carboxylic acid $\text{HO}_2\text{CCO}_2\text{H}$ reacts with amine $\text{H}_2\text{NCH}_2\text{CH}_2\text{NH}_2$. The $-\text{OH}$ from the acid and $-\text{H}$ from the amine are lost as water, leaving $-\text{CO-NH}-$. Because both monomers are difunctional, the chain grows at both ends.

Extend to two repeat units**
Link diamine to dioic acid alternately: $-\text{NH-CH}_2\text{CH}_2\text{-NH-CO-CO}-$ then repeat again. Draw two such blocks in sequence with brackets or continuation bonds through the ends to show polymer Z is a polyamide.

Final answer: Polyamide with repeat: $-[\text{NHCH}_2\text{CH}_2\text{NHCOCO}]-$ shown as two linked units with continuation bonds, containing amide $-\text{CONH}-$ groups. e.g. $-[\text{NHCH}_2\text{CH}_2\text{NHCOCO}]-[\text{NHCH}_2\text{CH}_2\text{NHCOCO}]-$

hints: Notice a small molecule, water, is lost each time the amide link forms, which distinguishes this from addition polymerisation.
walkthrough:
Classify by small molecule loss**
Each amide bond formation eliminates water. Polymerisation with loss of a small molecule is condensation polymerisation, also described mechanistically as addition-elimination at the carbonyl carbon.
Final answer: condensation (addition-elimination)

hints: Think of a polymer with a non-polar all carbon backbone and no hydrolysable amide or ester links, such as a common addition polymer.
walkthrough:
Pick a C-C chain polymer**
Polymer Z has polar amide links that can be hydrolysed, so it biodegrades. A polymer like poly(ethene), PVC or polystyrene has only strong non-polar C-C bonds with no site for hydrolysis, so micro-organisms cannot break it down and it is non-biodegradable.
Final answer: poly(ethene) / poly(propene) / PVC / polystyrene (any polyalkene, allow Kevlar)
